structured.name: Iceland
structured._source: wikidata (CC0); landBorders + naturalResources from CIA World Factbook (public domain)

prose.hook: Iceland is an island in the North Atlantic, between the Greenland Sea and the open ocean northwest of the United Kingdom, with no land border with any country. It sits directly on a volcanic hotspot, and that single geological fact shapes almost everything else: its hazards, its energy, and an economy built on fish, aluminium smelting and tourism rather than on minerals it does not have.
prose.physicalGeography: Mostly plateau, broken by mountain peaks and icefields, with a coast deeply indented by bays and fjords. It lies between the Greenland Sea and the North Atlantic Ocean, northwest of the United Kingdom, and has no land borders.
prose.climate: Temperate rather than arctic, despite the latitude, because the North Atlantic Current moderates it — winters are mild and windy, summers damp and cool. The more serious hazards are geological: Iceland sits on a hotspot with severe volcanic activity. Eyjafjallajökull erupted in 2010, throwing ash high enough to disrupt European air traffic for days, and scientists continue to monitor Katla, which has a high probability of eruption.
prose.economy: A high-income island economy that is not an EU member but is integrated into the European market through the European Economic Area. Tourism, fishing and aluminium smelting dominate, which leaves the country exposed both to swings in demand and to disruption from volcanic activity. Exports are led by aluminium, fish, orthopaedic appliances, animal meal and iron alloys. Inflation has run above target, and barriers to foreign business access have made diversification harder.
prose.peopleAndCulture: Icelandic is the official language, with English, Polish, other Nordic languages and German also spoken. The population is around 79% Icelandic with a Polish community of about 6%, plus Danish and Ukrainian residents. The Evangelical Lutheran Church of Iceland is the official church at roughly 59%; notably, about 8% report no religion and a further 19% are unspecified or belong to other groups, including a small but recognised pagan worship community.
